questions.q: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.why: It opened on 9 November 1989, and Germany was formally reunified less than a year later, in October 1990.

questions.q: Which civilisation built the mountain citadel of Machu Picchu?
questions.why: It was built in the 15th century in the Andes of Peru, probably as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti.

questions.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.why: He stepped onto the lunar surface on 21 July 1969 (UTC) during the Apollo 11 mission.

questions.q: In which year did the First World War begin?
questions.why: It broke out weeks after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in June 1914.

questions.q: Which ocean liner sank on its maiden voyage in April 1912?
questions.why: It struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic on its way from Southampton to New York; over 1,500 people died.

questions.q: Which ancient wonder stood at the harbour of Rhodes?
questions.why: The giant bronze statue of the sun god Helios was toppled by an earthquake around 226 BC.

questions.q: Who introduced movable-type printing to Europe around 1440?
questions.why: Working in Mainz, he produced the famous Gutenberg Bible in the 1450s.

questions.q: Which Roman city was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79?
questions.why: The ash preserved the city so well that excavations since the 18th century reveal daily Roman life.

questions.q: Whose expedition made the first circumnavigation of the globe, completed in 1522?
questions.why: He was killed in the Philippines in 1521; Juan Sebastian Elcano brought the last ship home to Spain.

questions.q: Which people developed cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems?
questions.why: Wedge-shaped marks were pressed into clay tablets in Mesopotamia from around 3200 BC.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.why: She shared the 1903 Physics prize, then won Chemistry in 1911; Bertha von Suttner won the Peace prize in 1905.

questions.q: Under which dynasty was Beijing's Forbidden City built?
questions.why: The Yongle Emperor had it built between 1406 and 1420 when he moved the capital to Beijing.

questions.q: Which treaty, signed in 1919, ended the war between Germany and the Allies?
questions.why: It was signed in the Hall of Mirrors on 28 June 1919, five years to the day after Franz Ferdinand's assassination.

questions.q: Who became the first emperor of a unified China in 221 BC?
questions.why: He standardised writing, coins and weights, and was buried with the famous Terracotta Army.

questions.q: Which city's great ancient library was founded under the Ptolemaic dynasty?
questions.why: The Ptolemies, Greek rulers of Egypt after Alexander, made it the leading centre of scholarship of its age.

questions.q: Mansa Musa, famed for his wealth and his pilgrimage to Mecca, ruled which empire?
questions.why: His lavish journey in 1324 spread so much gold through Cairo that its value there fell for years.

questions.q: Which Cambodian temple complex was built under King Suryavarman II?
questions.why: Built in the early 12th century and first dedicated to Vishnu, it is the largest religious monument in the world.

questions.q: Which Indian emperor embraced Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga war?
questions.why: Horrified by the carnage, he spread Buddhist ideals through edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire.

questions.q: Which leader founded the Mongol Empire in 1206?
questions.why: Born Temujin, he united the Mongol tribes; his empire became the largest contiguous land empire in history.

questions.q: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
questions.why: Greece was chosen to honour the ancient Games held at Olympia; the first modern marathon was run there.

questions.q: Which Japanese era began in 1868 with the restoration of imperial rule?
questions.why: It ended over 250 years of Tokugawa shogunate rule and launched Japan's rapid industrialisation.

questions.q: Whose nearly intact tomb did Howard Carter find in Egypt in 1922?
questions.why: The boy king's tomb in the Valley of the Kings held over 5,000 objects, including his gold funerary mask.

questions.q: The Rosetta Stone was key to deciphering which script?
questions.why: It carries one decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek; Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822.

questions.q: Suleiman the Magnificent ruled which empire in the 16th century?
questions.why: He reigned from 1520 to 1566, the longest of any Ottoman sultan, and is known in Turkey as the Lawgiver.

questions.q: Which Greek city-state trained its boys for war in a system called the agoge?
questions.why: Boys left home at about seven to live in barracks, where they were toughened by hardship and drilled in combat.

questions.q: Which is the longest river in Africa?
questions.why: It flows north for about 6,650 km and empties into the Mediterranean through a delta in Egypt.

questions.q: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.why: It was purpose-built as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne; Parliament moved there in 1927.

questions.q: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.why: It covers about a third of the planet's surface, more than all the land areas combined.

questions.q: In which mountain range does Mount Everest stand?
questions.why: Ten of the fourteen peaks above 8,000 m are in this range; the other four are in the nearby Karakoram.

questions.q: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.why: It spans about 9 million km2 of North Africa; only the cold polar deserts are larger.

questions.q: In which country is the city of Marrakesh?
questions.why: Founded in the 11th century by the Almoravids, it lies at the foot of the Atlas Mountains.

questions.q: What is the capital of Canada?
questions.why: Queen Victoria chose it in 1857, partly because it sat on the border between English and French Canada.

questions.q: What is the capital of New Zealand?
questions.why: It replaced Auckland in 1865 thanks to its central position between the North and South Islands.

questions.q: Which is the largest country in South America by area?
questions.why: It covers almost half of the continent and borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.

questions.q: Which is the smallest country in the world by area?
questions.why: An enclave within Rome of about 0.44 km2, it has been an independent state since the Lateran Treaty of 1929.

questions.q: Which strait connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean?
questions.why: At its narrowest it is only about 14 km wide, separating Spain from Morocco.

questions.q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
questions.why: This Siberian lake is over 1,600 m deep and holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water.

questions.q: Which river flows through the city of Baghdad?
questions.why: With the Euphrates it framed ancient Mesopotamia, whose name means the land between the rivers.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain in Africa?
questions.why: This dormant volcano in Tanzania rises to 5,895 m and still carries glaciers near the equator.

questions.q: Which of these South American countries is landlocked?
questions.why: It and Bolivia are the only landlocked countries in South America; it reaches the sea via the Parana river.

questions.q: What is the capital of Turkey?
questions.why: Ataturk made it the capital in 1923, preferring a central Anatolian city to the old imperial seat.

questions.q: Addis Ababa is the capital of which country?
questions.why: Its name means new flower in Amharic, and it hosts the headquarters of the African Union.

questions.q: Which river flows through Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade?
questions.why: It rises in Germany's Black Forest and flows through or along ten countries before reaching the Black Sea.

questions.q: Not counting Australia, which is the largest island in the world?
questions.why: About four fifths of it lies under an ice sheet up to 3 km thick.

questions.q: Lake Titicaca lies on the border of Peru and which other country?
questions.why: At about 3,800 m above sea level, it is often called the highest navigable lake in the world.

questions.q: In which country is the Okavango Delta?
questions.why: The river never reaches the sea: it fans out and evaporates in the Kalahari, creating a vast wetland.

questions.q: Which is the longest river in Europe?
questions.why: Flowing about 3,500 km entirely within Russia, it empties into the Caspian Sea.

questions.q: What is the capital of Mongolia?
questions.why: Its average annual temperature is below freezing, making it the coldest national capital in the world.

questions.q: Which strait separates Asia from North America?
questions.why: Only about 82 km wide, it lies between Russia's Chukotka and Alaska and is named after explorer Vitus Bering.

questions.q: Which city was the capital of Brazil before Brasilia?
questions.why: The capital moved inland to the newly built Brasilia in 1960 to encourage development of the interior.

questions.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
questions.why: The symbol comes from the Latin word for gold, aurum.

questions.q: Which planet orbits closest to the Sun?
questions.why: Mercury completes one orbit in about 88 Earth days, the shortest year of any planet.

questions.q: Which gas do plants take in from the air to carry out photosynthesis?
questions.why: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugars, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

questions.q: At sea level, at what temperature does pure water boil?
questions.why: The boiling point drops at altitude because air pressure is lower, so water boils below 100 degrees in the mountains.

questions.q: Which natural material is the hardest?
questions.why: Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs hardness scale; corundum, the mineral of rubies and sapphires, scores 9.

questions.q: Which is the largest planet in the Solar System?
questions.why: Jupiter is a gas giant with more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined.

questions.q: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.why: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the Solar System's mass, so its gravitational pull dominates the planets' paths.

questions.q: In plant and animal cells, which structure holds most of the DNA?
questions.why: The nucleus stores chromosomes; small amounts of DNA are also found in mitochondria and, in plants, chloroplasts.

questions.q: Which particle in an atom carries a negative electric charge?
questions.why: Electrons surround the nucleus, whose protons are positive and whose neutrons carry no charge.

questions.q: Which vitamin does human skin produce when exposed to sunlight?
questions.why: Ultraviolet B light triggers its production in the skin, and the body needs it to absorb calcium for healthy bones.

questions.q: Who published the general theory of relativity in 1915?
questions.why: It describes gravity as the curving of space and time by mass, refining Newton's earlier law of gravitation.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.why: It is named after the German physicist Georg Ohm, who related voltage, current and resistance.

questions.q: Which element has the atomic number 1?
questions.why: Its atom has a single proton, and it is the most abundant element in the universe.

questions.q: Roughly how long does light from the Sun take to reach Earth?
questions.why: Light covers the roughly 150 million km between the Sun and Earth at about 300,000 km per second.

questions.q: Which scientist worked out the basic laws of heredity by breeding pea plants?
questions.why: Mendel, a monk in Brno, published his results in 1866, but their importance was only recognised around 1900.

questions.q: Which part of the blood carries most of the oxygen around the body?
questions.why: Red blood cells are packed with haemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that binds oxygen in the lungs.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water at 25 degrees Celsius?
questions.why: Pure water is neutral: it holds equal amounts of hydrogen and hydroxide ions.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula of common table salt?
questions.why: Table salt is sodium chloride, a crystal made of sodium and chloride ions in equal numbers.

questions.q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928 after noticing mould killing bacteria?
questions.why: Fleming saw that a Penicillium mould stopped bacteria growing; the drug was mass-produced in the 1940s.

questions.q: Which part of a cell produces most of its usable energy?
questions.why: Mitochondria make ATP through cellular respiration, and they carry their own small set of DNA.

questions.q: What is the approximate speed of light in a vacuum?
questions.why: At that speed, light could circle Earth about seven and a half times in one second.

questions.q: Which noble gas is the most abundant in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.why: Argon makes up almost 1% of the air; most of it comes from the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in rocks.

questions.q: Which element is the most abundant in Earth's crust by mass?
questions.why: Oxygen makes up nearly half of the crust's mass, mostly bound with silicon in silicate minerals.

questions.q: Which planet spins almost on its side, with its axis tilted about 98 degrees?
questions.why: Because of this tilt, each pole of Uranus gets about 42 Earth years of continuous sunlight, then as long in darkness.

questions.q: Which metal is liquid at a normal room temperature of 20 degrees Celsius?
questions.why: Mercury melts at about -39 degrees Celsius; gallium and caesium melt only at around 30 degrees.

questions.q: Which bird can fly backwards?
questions.why: Hummingbirds can hover and even fly backwards by sweeping their wings in a figure-of-eight motion.

questions.q: Which is the largest living land animal?
questions.why: Large African bush elephant males can weigh around 6 tonnes, more than any other animal living on land.

questions.q: How many legs does a spider have?
questions.why: Spiders are arachnids, not insects; insects have six legs and three body parts.

questions.q: What do honeybees collect from flowers to make honey?
questions.why: Bees evaporate water from the sugary nectar and add enzymes; the pollen they gather is mainly food for larvae.

questions.q: Which gas makes up most of the air in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.why: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with argon and other gases making up the rest.

questions.q: Which is the largest animal living today?
questions.why: Blue whales can exceed 25 m in length, and they feed almost entirely on tiny krill.

questions.q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
questions.why: A newborn kangaroo is only about the size of a bean and finishes developing in its mother's pouch.

questions.q: To which group of animals do frogs belong?
questions.why: Most frogs start life as tadpoles breathing with gills in water, then develop lungs and legs.

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level?
questions.why: Everest stands on the border of Nepal and China, at nearly 8,850 m above sea level.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies and forecasts the weather called?
questions.why: The word comes from the Greek meteoros, meaning high in the air.

questions.q: Which instrument measures air pressure?
questions.why: Falling pressure often signals unsettled weather, while rising pressure usually brings calmer conditions.

questions.q: What is the change from caterpillar to butterfly called?
questions.why: Inside the chrysalis, much of the caterpillar's body is broken down and rebuilt into the adult form.

questions.q: What are clouds mainly made of?
questions.why: Water vapour is invisible; clouds form when it cools and condenses into tiny droplets or ice crystals.

questions.q: Which is the largest living bird?
questions.why: Ostriches cannot fly, but they can stand over 2 m tall and lay the largest eggs of any living bird.

questions.q: What is the innermost layer of the Earth?
questions.why: It is a ball of mostly iron and nickel that stays solid despite its heat because of the enormous pressure.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.why: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and the third pumps it around the rest of the body.

questions.q: Which type of rock forms when magma or lava cools and hardens?
questions.why: Granite forms from magma cooling slowly underground, while basalt forms from lava cooling quickly at the surface.

questions.q: What mainly causes the seasons on Earth?
questions.why: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during winter in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: Which pigment gives most plants their green colour?
questions.why: It absorbs mostly red and blue light for photosynthesis and reflects green light.

questions.q: What is an animal that eats only plants called?
questions.why: Many herbivores, such as cows, have long or multi-chambered digestive systems to break down tough plant matter.

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere is most of the ozone layer found?
questions.why: Ozone there absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation before it reaches the ground.

questions.q: Which supercontinent joined nearly all of Earth's land until about 200 million years ago?
questions.why: As it split apart, the Atlantic Ocean opened up, which is why South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces.

questions.q: Which are the only mammals capable of true powered flight?
questions.why: Their wings are skin stretched over long finger bones; the other animals listed can only glide.

questions.q: Which tree species grows the tallest in the world?
questions.why: Coast redwoods grow in fog-rich northern California, and the tallest measured exceed 115 m.

questions.q: What is the term for animals that are mainly active at dawn and dusk?
questions.why: The word comes from the Latin crepusculum, meaning twilight; rabbits and many deer behave this way.

questions.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.why: Leonardo worked on the portrait in the early 1500s; it has hung in the Louvre in Paris for most of the time since the French Revolution.

questions.q: Which painter created The Starry Night in 1889?
questions.why: Van Gogh painted it from his room at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, in southern France.

questions.q: Which sculptor created The Thinker?
questions.why: The figure was first conceived as part of The Gates of Hell, Rodin's large bronze door inspired by Dante's Inferno.

questions.q: Which composer set Schiller's poem Ode to Joy in the finale of his Ninth Symphony?
questions.why: Premiered in Vienna in 1824, it was among the first major symphonies to use a choir and vocal soloists.

questions.q: How many keys does a standard modern piano have?
questions.why: The 52 white and 36 black keys span just over seven octaves, from A0 to C8.

questions.q: In which city stands the Sagrada Família basilica designed by Antoni Gaudí?
questions.why: Construction began in 1882 and Gaudí devoted the last decades of his life to it; he is buried in its crypt.

questions.q: Which art movement did Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque develop in the early 1900s?
questions.why: Cubism broke objects into geometric planes and showed several viewpoints at once on a single flat canvas.

questions.q: Who composed the set of violin concertos known as The Four Seasons?
questions.why: Published in 1725, each of the four concertos came with a sonnet describing the season it depicts.

questions.q: Who painted The Scream?
questions.why: The Norwegian artist made several versions from 1893 onwards, in paint, pastel and as a lithograph.

questions.q: How many lines make up a standard musical staff?
questions.why: Notes sit on the lines or in the four spaces between them, and ledger lines extend the range above or below.

questions.q: Which Japanese artist made the woodblock print The Great Wave off Kanagawa?
questions.why: It is part of his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, and the mountain appears small beneath the wave.

questions.q: Which composer wrote the opera The Magic Flute?
questions.why: It premiered in Vienna in September 1791, just over two months before Mozart's death at the age of 35.

questions.q: Which architect designed the titanium-clad Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao?
questions.why: Opened in 1997, its success in reviving the city gave rise to the expression "the Bilbao effect".

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor had the Taj Mahal built in Agra?
questions.why: He built the white marble mausoleum in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631.

questions.q: Who directed the 1954 Japanese film Seven Samurai?
questions.why: Its story of villagers hiring warriors was remade as the Western The Magnificent Seven in 1960.

questions.q: Which silent film star created the character known as the Tramp?
questions.why: The bowler hat, cane, baggy trousers and small moustache first appeared on screen in 1914.

questions.q: Which Italian musical term tells performers to get gradually louder?
questions.why: The word means "growing"; its opposite, diminuendo or decrescendo, asks for a gradual softening.

questions.q: Which composer wrote the operas La traviata and Aida?
questions.why: Aida was commissioned by the ruler of Egypt and premiered at the Cairo opera house in 1871.

questions.q: Who painted Girl with a Pearl Earring?
questions.why: The Delft painter left only around 35 known works; this one hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

questions.q: In which country was the Bauhaus school of art and design founded in 1919?
questions.why: Walter Gropius founded it in Weimar; it later moved to Dessau and then Berlin before closing in 1933.

questions.q: How many strings does a standard violin have?
questions.why: They are tuned in fifths, G, D, A and E, from the lowest to the highest.

questions.q: Which composer's ballet The Rite of Spring caused an uproar at its 1913 Paris premiere?
questions.why: Its clashing rhythms and Nijinsky's choreography provoked such noise that the dancers struggled to hear the orchestra.

questions.q: Which painter made a long series of water lily paintings in his garden at Giverny?
questions.why: He painted the pond he had created there for about the last thirty years of his life, around 250 times.

questions.q: Which 1927 silent film by Fritz Lang depicts a futuristic city of workers and rulers?
questions.why: It was among the most expensive films of its time, and its robot double of the heroine Maria became a science fiction icon.

questions.q: What is the technique of painting on fresh, wet lime plaster called?
questions.why: The pigments bind as the plaster dries, which is how Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

questions.q: Who wrote the novel Don Quixote?
questions.why: Its two parts appeared in 1605 and 1615, and it is often called the first modern novel.

questions.q: Who wrote the novel War and Peace?
questions.why: Set during the Napoleonic Wars, it follows several aristocratic families and has hundreds of characters.

questions.q: In which Italian city is Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet set?
questions.why: Romeo is banished from it to nearby Mantua, which is why he misses the message about Juliet's plan.

questions.q: Which writer created the fictional town of Macondo?
questions.why: Macondo is the setting of One Hundred Years of Solitude, published in 1967, a landmark of magical realism.

questions.q: What is the name of Don Quixote's loyal squire?
questions.why: The down-to-earth peasant rides a donkey beside the knight, whose own horse is called Rocinante.

questions.q: What is a word or phrase that reads the same backwards and forwards called?
questions.why: The term comes from Greek words meaning "running back again"; "level" and "radar" are examples.

questions.q: In which language did Dante write the Divine Comedy?
questions.why: Choosing the vernacular over Latin was bold, and the poem helped make Tuscan the basis of standard Italian.

questions.q: Which author created the detective Hercule Poirot?
questions.why: Poirot, a retired Belgian police officer, first appeared in The Mysterious Affair at Styles in 1920.

questions.q: In which city does Georges Simenon's Inspector Maigret mainly work?
questions.why: Maigret is a commissaire of the Paris police, based at the famous headquarters on the Quai des Orfèvres.

questions.q: Which author wrote The Metamorphosis, in which Gregor Samsa wakes up as a giant insect?
questions.why: The novella was published in German in 1915; Kafka lived in Prague and wrote in German.

questions.q: How many letters does the modern Greek alphabet have?
questions.why: It runs from alpha to omega, which is why "alpha and omega" means the beginning and the end.

questions.q: In Homer's Odyssey, which island is the home of Odysseus?
questions.why: The epic tells of his ten-year journey home after the Trojan War, back to his wife Penelope.

questions.q: Who wrote the novel Les Misérables?
questions.why: Published in 1862, it follows the former convict Jean Valjean, pursued for years by Inspector Javert.

questions.q: Which author wrote Pride and Prejudice?
questions.why: Published in 1813, it was first credited only to "the author of Sense and Sensibility".

questions.q: What is the short Japanese poem of 5, 7 and 5 sound units, often with a seasonal word, called?
questions.why: Matsuo Bashō, in the 17th century, is the best-known master of the form; the tanka is longer, at 31 units.

questions.q: How many lines does a traditional sonnet have?
questions.why: The form was popularised by Petrarch in 14th-century Italy before spreading across European poetry.

questions.q: The word "robot" first appeared in a 1920 play written in which language?
questions.why: It comes from Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. and is based on "robota", meaning forced labour.

questions.q: Who wrote the 1958 novel Things Fall Apart, set among the Igbo of Nigeria?
questions.why: It follows the warrior Okonkwo and is one of the most widely read novels from Africa.

questions.q: Who wrote The Tale of Genji, often called one of the world's first novels?
questions.why: She was a lady at the Japanese imperial court and wrote it in the early 11th century.

questions.q: What is an abbreviation pronounced as a word, such as NATO or laser, called?
questions.why: An initialism like BBC or UN is instead spoken letter by letter.

questions.q: From which language does the word "kindergarten" come?
questions.why: Friedrich Fröbel coined it in 1840: it literally means "children's garden".

questions.q: Who wrote the novel Crime and Punishment?
questions.why: Published in 1866, it follows the student Raskolnikov in Saint Petersburg after he commits a murder.

questions.q: In Moby-Dick, which captain obsessively hunts the white whale?
questions.why: Ishmael narrates the story, Queequeg is a harpooner and Starbuck is the first mate of the ship Pequod.

questions.q: Which part of speech describes or modifies a noun?
questions.why: In "a red apple", red is the adjective; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs instead.

questions.q: Who created the constructed language Esperanto?
questions.why: He published it in 1887 under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, meaning "one who hopes".

questions.q: How many players does each team have on the field in a football (soccer) match?
questions.why: A team fields ten outfield players plus one goalkeeper; a match cannot start with fewer than seven.

questions.q: How many squares are there on a chessboard?
questions.why: The board is 8 by 8, with alternating light and dark squares and a light square in each player's right-hand corner.

questions.q: In tennis, what word is used for a score of zero?
questions.why: Tennis scoring runs love, 15, 30, 40, then game, with deuce when both players reach 40.

questions.q: How many interlocking rings appear on the Olympic flag?
questions.why: Designed by Pierre de Coubertin in 1913, the rings stand for the union of the inhabited continents.

questions.q: Which chess piece can only ever move diagonally?
questions.why: Because of this, each bishop stays on squares of one colour for the whole game.

questions.q: In basketball, how many points is a successful shot from beyond the arc worth?
questions.why: Shots inside the arc score two points, and free throws score one point each.

questions.q: How many cards are in a standard deck, not counting jokers?
questions.why: The deck has four suits of 13 cards each: ace, numbers 2 to 10, jack, queen and king.

questions.q: In chess, which piece can jump over other pieces?
questions.why: It moves in an L shape, two squares one way then one at a right angle, whatever stands in between.

questions.q: How many players per team are on the court at once in indoor volleyball?
questions.why: Players rotate one position clockwise each time their team wins back the serve.

questions.q: In golf, what is a score of one stroke under par on a hole called?
questions.why: An eagle is two under par, while a bogey is one stroke over par.

questions.q: What is the chess move in which the king and a rook move at the same time?
questions.why: It is allowed only if neither piece has moved and the king is not in, passing through, or landing in check.

questions.q: How many points is the black ball worth in snooker?
questions.why: It is the highest-value colour; the others are yellow 2, green 3, brown 4, blue 5 and pink 6.

questions.q: In rugby union, how many points is a try worth?
questions.why: A try can be followed by a conversion kick worth two more points.

questions.q: In whose honour were the ancient Olympic Games held?
questions.why: The Games took place at Olympia, home of a great temple to Zeus with a famous statue of the god.

questions.q: Which board game uses the terms ko and atari?
questions.why: Atari means a group has only one liberty left, and the ko rule stops endless repeated captures.

questions.q: What is the highest score possible with a single dart on a standard dartboard?
questions.why: It comes from the treble ring of the 20 segment; the bullseye is worth only 50.

questions.q: What is the official distance of a marathon?
questions.why: The distance comes from the 1908 London Olympics course, which ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium.

questions.q: Which sport is played with a shuttlecock?
questions.why: A traditional shuttlecock has 16 overlapping feathers set in a rounded cork base.

questions.q: How many checkers does each player start with in backgammon?
questions.why: Each player races their checkers around the 24 points and bears them off the board to win.

questions.q: In judo, what is the term for a full point that ends the contest at once?
questions.why: An ippon can be scored by a clean throw onto the back, a pin, or a submission.

questions.q: In standard chess notation, which letter stands for the knight?
questions.why: K is already taken by the king, so the knight is written as N in English notation.

questions.q: Where were the first Winter Olympic Games held, in 1924?
questions.why: The French Alpine town hosted about 250 athletes from 16 nations below Mont Blanc.

questions.q: How many riders are on each team in a polo match?
questions.why: Each rider usually wears a number from 1 to 4 that matches their position on the field.

questions.q: In cricket, how many legal balls make up a standard over?
questions.why: After each over, bowling switches to the opposite end of the pitch and to a different bowler.

questions.q: How many squares are there on a standard Scrabble board?
questions.why: The board is a 15 by 15 grid, with the centre square marked by a star for the first word.

questions.q: How many days are there in a leap year?
questions.why: The extra day, 29 February, keeps the calendar in step with the roughly 365.24-day solar year.

questions.q: What is the main ingredient of guacamole?
questions.why: The dip comes from Mexico, and its name derives from the Nahuatl word ahuacamolli.

questions.q: Feta cheese comes from which country?
questions.why: In the EU, feta is a protected name: it must be made in Greece from sheep's or sheep and goat milk.

questions.q: How many minutes are there in a day?
questions.why: A day has 24 hours of 60 minutes each, so 24 times 60 gives the total.

questions.q: Paella is a traditional rice dish from which country?
questions.why: It originated around Valencia and is named after the wide, shallow pan it is cooked in.

questions.q: How many grams are there in a kilogram?
questions.why: The prefix kilo comes from the Greek for thousand, as in kilometre and kilowatt.

questions.q: Which month is the shortest of the year?
questions.why: It has 28 days, or 29 in a leap year; every other month has 30 or 31 days.

questions.q: Hummus is made mainly from which ingredient?
questions.why: The chickpeas are blended with tahini, a paste of sesame seeds, plus lemon juice and garlic.

questions.q: Tofu is made from the curdled milk of which bean?
questions.why: Soy milk is curdled, much like cheese-making, and the curds are pressed into blocks.

questions.q: How many seconds are there in an hour?
questions.why: Dividing the hour by 60, then by 60 again, comes from Babylonian base-60 counting, also behind the 360 degrees of a circle.

questions.q: Which spice is made from the dried stigmas of a crocus flower?
questions.why: Each flower has just three stigmas, picked by hand, which is why the spice is so costly.

questions.q: Which vegetable is the base of the most common kind of kimchi?
questions.why: The cabbage is salted, then fermented with chilli, garlic, ginger and often fish sauce.

questions.q: Which herb is the main ingredient of pesto alla genovese?
questions.why: It is ground with pine nuts, garlic, olive oil and hard cheese, traditionally in a marble mortar.

questions.q: Marzipan is made mainly from sugar and which nut?
questions.why: The ground nuts and sugar form a paste that is easy to colour and shape into small figures.

questions.q: Which calendar did the Gregorian calendar replace?
questions.why: The older calendar ran about 11 minutes a year too long, so dates slowly drifted from the seasons.

questions.q: Couscous is traditionally made from which grain?
questions.why: Semolina from durum wheat is moistened and rolled into tiny grains, then steamed.

questions.q: Halloumi cheese traditionally comes from which island?
questions.why: Its high melting point means it can be grilled or fried without losing its shape.

questions.q: Besides kilocalories, which unit is used for the energy in food?
questions.why: One kilocalorie equals about 4.184 kilojoules, the SI unit used on many food labels.

questions.q: Prunes are the dried fruit of which tree?
questions.why: Not every plum works: prunes come from varieties sweet enough to dry without fermenting.

questions.q: Japanese sake is brewed from which grain?
questions.why: The rice is polished to remove its outer layers, then fermented with koji mould and yeast.

questions.q: In which country was paper first made from plant fibres?
questions.why: Papyrus from Egypt is older, but it is made from pressed strips of reed, not from pulped fibres.

questions.q: The burrs of which plant inspired the invention of Velcro?
questions.why: In 1941 George de Mestral saw how the burrs' tiny hooks gripped his dog's fur and his clothes.

questions.q: In which year was the Gregorian calendar first introduced?
questions.why: To realign the dates, ten days were skipped: 4 October 1582 was followed by 15 October.

questions.q: Which unit of volume is equal to one cubic decimetre?
questions.why: A cube 10 cm on each side holds exactly one litre, so 1,000 of them fill a cubic metre.

questions.q: Ghee, widely used in South Asian cooking, is made from what?
questions.why: The butter is simmered until the water evaporates and milk solids are removed, leaving pure butterfat.
